I work for a company that's attempting to migrate its rich (desktop) applications to the web. The application I was tasked with migrating is not a large one, but that's not to say it's lightweight, either. Before minification of all the scripts/css involved, initial page size is around 2.2 MB (including all the calls it makes out to the application server to get values/user information/etc). The scripts that it loads include Crypto.js, Chart.js, Angular.js (and a whole bunch of extensions for it), a custom script I wrote to get some global values, and the webapp script itself. These files run at around 1.9MB before minification. After minification, the entire page runs at something like 1.2 to 1.3 MB on initial load (largely because Angular.js contains about 900KB of comments/whitespace). All of this is fetched and renders to the screen in around a second, sometimes more. And I even put a splash screen in to hide most of the rendering from the end user and make the entire thing look much nicer/professional (my supervisor calls it flair or turd lacquer, depending on the day).

Now, a news article doesn't really do a lot. It's meant to just sit there and get rendered, then never be modified. The webapp that I made is smaller than modern news articles and can do a lot more than any news article can or should do - even before minification.

I think part of the problem with news articles (besides the copious amount of ads/clickbait titles on the page that obscure the article) is that their developers aren't willing to hard-code their own workarounds for various browsers - like I've had to do at times in my webapp - instead they just grab another JS library to go and fix it for them, and even if all they need is 3 lines from the library, they'll put the entire script in there. Before long, you've got jQuery, a few jQuery plugins, Modernizr.js, and lord knows what else in your page. Even when minified, all those are probably about 1.5 MB. Then you've got your own custom script for the news article, and that's probably another 300 to 500 kilobytes because the people making these news sites don't know a lot about optimization.

Add in all the ads, clickbait links, and images, and a single news article is not only bloated, but very far from performant. Some news articles I've seen that rely on deferred rendering of elements can take 5-10 seconds to render everything on my PC.

The problem was that the technology was so unfamiliar that people just didn't dare touch it. Since the people in the orphanage didn't know how to service them the panels just lay there until finally somebody stole them, probably to use as a chicken coup door.

The lesson here is that the technology needs to be appropriate and it must be delivered with people who know how to install and maintain it.
